questions.q: Why do model artifacts and training checkpoints need the same backup and replication discipline as a production database?
options: They are both critical assets whose loss is costly — a lost model artifact can mean an outage, and a lost checkpoint can mean redoing weeks of GPU-hours
They don't — only databases genuinely need disaster recovery planning
Model artifacts are automatically backed up by every cloud provider with no configuration needed
Training checkpoints are cheap to regenerate instantly, so backup is optional
questions.explain: Both are exactly as critical as a production database and exactly as capable of permanent loss if not deliberately backed up and replicated.

questions.q: Why should the production model registry typically have a near-zero RPO?
options: Model registries never actually need to be restored
Registries change too frequently to ever replicate reliably
It's cheaper not to replicate the registry at all
Served models rarely change, so near-zero-RPO replication is cheap relative to the cost of an outage with no known-good model to fail back to
questions.explain: Because the registry changes infrequently, synchronous or near-synchronous replication is affordable, and the alternative — losing the only known-good served model — is far more costly.

questions.q: Why can training checkpoints tolerate a larger RPO than the production model registry?
options: Checkpoints are never actually needed for recovery
The cost of losing the most recent checkpoint is bounded and known — it's the GPU-hours since the last successful save, not an indefinite loss
Checkpoints are automatically replicated synchronously by default on every cloud
Training runs cannot be resumed from a checkpoint under any circumstances
questions.explain: Losing a checkpoint costs a known, bounded amount of re-training time, which is a different and more tolerable risk than losing the actively-served production model.

questions.q: What failure mode must a disaster recovery plan for GPU-backed AI infrastructure account for that a typical stateless-service DR plan doesn't?
options: DNS propagation delays, which are unique to AI workloads
TLS certificate renewal, which only affects machine learning services
The failover region might not have the needed GPU SKU available, even if networking, data replication, and DNS all work correctly
The requirement that all failover regions must be on the same continent
questions.explain: Ordinary DR planning assumes the secondary region can simply provide equivalent compute on demand; that assumption breaks for GPU-backed workloads if the failover region's GPU capacity isn't actually available.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should a realistic DR runbook for ML infrastructure actually test?
options: Only that backup files exist in object storage, with no further verification
Nothing — DR plans for ML infrastructure cannot be meaningfully tested
Only whether the training job's Docker image still builds successfully
Restoring a model from its replica and confirming correct predictions, resuming training from a checkpoint, and failing inference over to reserved or degraded-mode capacity within its latency SLOs
questions.explain: Each of those is a distinct test protecting against a different failure mode, and a DR plan that's never exercised this way is effectively a guess.
